name: PT Indo Acidatama Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indo Acidatama: a molasses converter priced for a margin that has already gone
frontmatter.summary: We initiate on Indo Acidatama at BUY with a target of Rp169. The company ferments molasses into ethanol at one Central Java plant and sells most of it domestically. It earned a thirty per cent gross margin in the first nine months of 2026, yet the shares trade below pre-revaluation book and barely above our trough-margin bear case. The market treats that margin as a spike; we think it fades, but not that far.
thesis: The margin is a molasses event, but not the regulated leg that passes through: the fuel-grade margin is fixed in dollars, and the spike was earned on industrial, food-grade and export volumes, where the spread widened competitively.

Volume, not price, is the growth lever. The plant runs near its nameplate and the blend mandate adds domestic demand, but the company is not confirmed in the first allocation, so we credit only part of it.

The balance sheet carries the harvest. The seasonal molasses prepayment is funded by a revolver, so the September reporting date shows IDR86.6bn of short-term bank loans against IDR18.6bn of cash, while the same cycle swings the balance back to net cash by the following June. The debt line is a calendar, and the equity is real.

Cash conversion swings with the harvest, and the dividend is a floor, not a policy. Operating cash flow was negative in FY2024, far above net profit in FY2025 on a working-capital release, and IDR30.2bn in the nine months of 2026; the family has paid a flat rupiah dividend through all of it.

The discount is governance and float, not the business. Two-thirds insider ownership and a float near the exchange minimum keep generalist money out; that is the risk and the reason the price is where it is.

Monthly bioethanol reference price, the marker for the domestic fuel-grade spread

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Indo Acidatama at **BUY** with a target of Rp169, a 70.5% total return from Rp100. Our base value is Rp173 and the probability-weighted target is Rp169, so the target is not the optimistic branch dressed up as a point estimate. The share price sits between our trough-margin bear case of Rp84 and our base value of Rp173, and far below our bull case of Rp248: the market is close to pricing a permanent return to the FY2024 gross margin, which is the central fact of this report [S4, S6].

The business is a single-site converter. It buys molasses from sugar mills, ferments it, distils the result into ethanol, and sells the ethanol into pharmaceutical, hospital, cosmetics, perfume and cigarette supply chains, into the spiritus trade, and as feedstock for acetic acid and ethyl acetate [S3]. The same site makes bio-organic fertiliser from the stillage and, in a normal year, oxidises part of the ethanol into acetic acid [S3]. In FY2025 ethanol supplied IDR1,066.0bn of the IDR1,256.4bn of sales, acetic acid IDR89.7bn and other products IDR100.7bn [S4, F11, F12, F13].

The margin is the whole story. Gross margin was 16.6% in FY2024, 24.8% in FY2025 and 29.7% in our FY2026E, which blends nine months of actual at a margin above thirty per cent with a softer fourth quarter [S4, S6]. The step-up is a feedstock event: molasses is the dominant cost, the cane harvest sets its price, and the regulated bioethanol reference price is itself built from a three-month molasses average, so the input passes into the selling price rather than compressing the spread [S10, F25, F26]. That is why we fade the margin rather than collapse it, and why the fade is a reversion to the top of the historical range rather than a return to the trough [S3, S4].

Three things move the value. First, the molasses price and the reference price built on it: together they set the spread on the fuel-grade volumes, and the feedstock alone sets the cost of everything else [S10, S3]. Second, volume: installed ethanol capacity is 78,825 kilolitres against 73,029 produced in FY2025, so there is headroom but not much, and the blend mandate is the only large source of new domestic demand [S3, S8, S9]. Third, the working-capital cycle: the company prepays for molasses at the harvest, funds it with a revolver, and unwinds it through the year, which makes the reported net cash position swing by more than a year of earnings [S6, F23].

The market disagrees with us on the durability of the margin, and it is not obviously wrong. What it appears to ignore is that the shares change hands below book value per share of Rp154, even after taking out the IDR165.3bn PSAK 16 revaluation surplus that sits in equity, and only just above our trough-margin bear case [S4, S6, F37]. Our answer is not that the margin holds at the peak; it is that even with the margin fading to 24.5% by FY2030E, the discounted cash flow is worth Rp152 a share, the EV/EBITDA leg agrees to within a point or two, and the P/E leg is about a seventh higher because it capitalises a peak year [S4].

Indo Acidatama operates one agro-chemical plant at Kemiri in Karanganyar, Central Java, on the Solo-Sragen road, and sells from an office in Jakarta [S3]. The site was built as PT Indo Alkohol Utama in the early nineteen-eighties, was renamed PT Indo Acidatama Chemical Industry, began commercial production at the end of that decade, merged with the already-listed PT Sarasa Nugraha in 2005 and took its present name in 2006 [S3]. It has been a public company under the SRSN code since that merger, classified in the basic chemicals industry [S3]. The company employed 409 people at the end of FY2025, up from a slightly smaller base a year earlier [S3].

The product set is narrow and the capacity is disclosed precisely. Annual ethanol capacity is 78,825 kilolitres, acetic acid capacity is 36.6 thousand tonnes, and a bio-organic fertiliser line runs alongside the distillation train [S3, F5, F6]. Ethanol is sold into pharmaceutical manufacturing, hospitals, cosmetics, perfume and cigarettes, as methylated spirit, as a base for alcoholic drinks, as gasohol, and as the raw material for acetic acid and ethyl acetate [S3]. Acetic acid goes into food vinegar, purified terephthalic acid, textiles, elastic thread and PVC film [S3]. The fertiliser brands are sold to rice, corn, vegetable, tobacco, tea and plantation growers [S3].

The production record shows a plant running close to its limit. Ethanol output was 73,029 kilolitres in FY2025 against 67,547 in FY2024, an increase the company attributes to the product-mix strategy rather than to new equipment [S3, F3, F4]. Fertiliser output fell over the same period, and the company did not produce ethyl acetate or acetic acid at all in FY2025, so the acetic acid revenue line is traded product rather than own manufacture [S3, F28]. That matters for the margin: the higher-value oxidation chain was switched off, and the profit and loss account is effectively an ethanol account with a trading overlay [S3, S4]. The idle plant is not written off: the 36.6 thousand tonne acetic acid line stays inside the fixed-asset block with no separate impairment recognised in FY2025 or in the nine months of 2026, and no impairment test is disclosed for it [S4, S6, F6]. The base case gives it no earnings but does not assume a write-down either; its carrying value is therefore tested in the price-to-book cross-check rather than in the cash flow, and a restart would be a revenue event, which is why the bull case carries a revenue shock and not a margin one [S3, S4, F6].

The customer mix is domestic-weighted with a material export book. In FY2025 ethanol sales were IDR685.4bn domestically and IDR380.6bn for export, against IDR658.6bn and IDR331.1bn respectively in FY2024, so roughly a third of ethanol revenue is earned in export markets [S4, F7, F8, F9, F10]. The company does not disclose destination countries in the annual report, but it describes its export strategy as quality control and delivery reliability rather than price [S3]. Domestic sales are made direct to end users as well as through distributors, and the company prices by customer specification, which is how a commodity molecule earns a non-commodity margin [S3].

The raw material is contracted, not bought on the spot. The company holds molasses purchase agreements with PT Kebon Agung and with the state plantation companies in Central and East Java, and it received contracts for 124 thousand tonnes for the 2025 harvest against 119.5 thousand tonnes for 2024 [S3, F14, F15]. Supply comes from about 29 suppliers across Central Java, East Java and outside Java [S3, F30]. The contracts are the moat: a mill's molasses has few alternative buyers, but a producer without a contract cannot run its plant. They are not, however, a full year's cover. The 124 thousand tonnes contracted for the 2025 harvest, converted at the 4.1 kilograms per litre in the ministry formula, supports about thirty thousand kilolitres of ethanol against the 73,029 produced, so the contracts cover roughly two-fifths of requirements and the balance is bought from the 29 suppliers [S3, F14, F26, F3, F30]. That matters twice: the moat is narrower than a headline contract implies, and the cost model cannot be a contracted-price model.

The ownership is concentrated in two families and their vehicles. At the end of FY2025 local individuals held 61.1% of the shares and local limited companies a further share, with foreign holders a rounding error [S3, F29]. The register names the Setijo and Budhi families and three family companies among the holders above five per cent, and the president director is a member of the Budhi family [S3]. Insider holdings are 65.9% and the free float is 31.9%, which is above the exchange minimum but far below what an index-tracking investor needs [S3].

Molasses is the syrup left after sugar is crystallised. A mill cannot sell it as food, so it is sold as a fermentation feedstock, and its price is set by the size of the cane crop and by competition from other fermenters, feed makers and distilleries. Fermenting molasses yields a dilute alcohol that is distilled to different purities: industrial grade for solvents and spiritus, food grade for drinks and cosmetics, and fuel grade for blending into petrol. The same plant can switch between grades, which is why producers talk about product mix rather than about a single price.

Indonesia's ethanol industry is small, and the part of it that can serve the fuel mandate is smaller still. The energy ministry puts the combined bioethanol capacity of the three producers it has cleared for fuel grade at about 26,000 kilolitres — an order of magnitude below what a national blend would need, and a third of Indo Acidatama's own 78,825 kilolitres [S9, S3, F35, F5]. The ministry's own demand arithmetic makes the gap explicit: a twenty per cent blend in 2028 would need between four and five hundred thousand kilolitres of ethanol, against a current feedstock pool of about seventy thousand [S7]. The government expects eleven new plants to close part of that gap, which tells you that the incumbents are not expected to fill it alone [S7].

The policy path is dated and staged. The five per cent blend became mandatory in the second half of 2026, initially in Jakarta, Central Java, East Java, West Java, Yogyakarta, Bali and Lampung, and only for non-subsidised fuel [S8, S9]. The energy minister has said the ten per cent blend will be mandated in 2027, with a first phase of ten to twenty per cent, and the ministry is preparing the technical rules [S11]. The feedstock must be domestic, which is a protection for local producers and a constraint on volume at the same time [S9]. Only three companies were identified as able to make fuel grade when the mandate was designed, and the combined capacity attributed to them is small [S9].

The pricing mechanism is the most important structural fact in the sector. The energy ministry sets a monthly market index price for bioethanol using a formula that multiplies the three-month average molasses price by a conversion factor and adds a fixed dollar margin per litre [S10, F26]. For November 2026 the index was set at 11,955 rupiah a litre on molasses of 1,816 rupiah a kilogram [S10, F24, F25]. The formula is cost-plus by construction: a rise in molasses lifts the reference price almost one for one, and the producer's reward for converting is the fixed dollar component, not the spread between input and output [S10].

That structure cuts both ways for Indo Acidatama. It protects the fuel-grade margin from a molasses spike, which is the risk the market usually assigns to a converter, but it also caps the upside: the company cannot earn more per litre simply because molasses is expensive [S10, F26]. The margin that matters is therefore the one on industrial, food-grade and export volumes, where prices are set by competition rather than by formula, and that is where the FY2025 and FY2026 margins were actually earned [S3, S4]. It also means the equity story is a volume story in fuel grade and a spread story everywhere else.

Competition is thin at the top and fragmented below it. The ministry identified only three fuel-grade producers with 26,000 kilolitres between them, while the company's own ethanol capacity is 78,825 kilolitres, so on the ministry's own arithmetic Indo Acidatama is either producing almost entirely non-fuel grade or is not one of the three. The second reading is the one the filing supports: a producer cleared for fuel grade would need an allocation, and no allocation has been published naming the company [S3, S9, F35, F5]. Either way it is a caution against assuming Indo Acidatama is an automatic beneficiary of the blend mandate. Below the fuel-grade tier, the competition is other molasses fermenters, importers of industrial ethanol and, in the food-grade niche, Brazilian and Chinese supply [S3].

The barriers are real but modest. A new entrant needs a molasses contract, a distillation train, food-safety and pharmaceutical manufacturing certifications, and a distribution relationship with end users who qualify suppliers [S3]. Indo Acidatama holds the food-safety system certification that superseded its hazard-control system, a halal certificate, and a pharmaceutical good-manufacturing-practice certificate, and it has held them long enough to be an incumbent supplier [S3]. Those certifications are the reason a pharmaceutical buyer does not switch on price alone, and they are the closest thing to a moat the company has [S3].

The demand side is split between a slow-growing industrial market and a policy-driven fuel market. Industrial and food-grade ethanol demand grows with the pharmaceutical, cosmetics and beverage economies, which is roughly nominal output growth [S3]. Fuel-grade demand is a policy variable that can move in steps, and the steps are large relative to the installed base [S7, S11]. The company's own outlook for 2026 is cautious on the industrial side, citing tight US monetary policy, a stronger dollar, higher funding costs and geopolitical energy risk, while calling the renewable-energy demand trend positive [S3].

The import-restriction regime is a two-sided influence the company names itself. It says the policy gives domestic industry an opportunity but can also create domestic supply shortages and requires capacity and efficiency investment to meet demand [S3]. For a producer that already runs near capacity, the protection helps price and the shortage hurts volume, and the net effect depends on whether the company can lift output [S3, F5, F3].

Indonesia's blend mandate is administered through a market index price rather than a fixed subsidy. The energy ministry publishes a monthly reference price for each biofuel, built from a published feedstock benchmark plus a conversion margin, and fuel distributors buy at that reference. Because the feedstock benchmark is a trailing average, the reference price lags the spot input cost, which means a producer's realised spread depends on where it bought feedstock relative to the average. That lag, not the level of either price, is what makes the quarterly margin move.

The five-year record is a commodity margin with a step change in the last two years. Revenue went from IDR977.7bn in FY2022 to IDR1,256.4bn in FY2025, while gross profit went from IDR185.7bn to IDR312.1bn and operating profit from IDR49.2bn to IDR120.3bn [S4]. The path was not smooth: FY2024 was the trough, with a gross margin of 16.6% and net profit of IDR22.5bn, and FY2025 recovered to 24.8% and IDR77.4bn [S4].

The nine months of 2026 are better again on margin and worse on revenue. Nine-month sales ran below the same period a year earlier, while the gross margin rose above thirty per cent against twenty-two per cent a year earlier [S6]. Operating profit for the nine months was well ahead of the board's own plan for the year, which had projected sales of IDR950.0bn and operating profit of IDR90.0bn [S3, F31, F32]. The company beat its plan by a wide margin because the molasses spread widened after the plan was written, not because volume grew [S3, S6].

The cost structure explains the operating leverage. Raw material usage in cost of goods sold was IDR670.0bn in FY2025, the overwhelming majority of the cost base, so a ten per cent move in molasses moves gross profit by roughly a third [S4, F16]. Operating expenses behave as a fixed block: selling costs are dominated by export freight and commission, and administration by salaries and depreciation [S4]. That is why a revenue decline of the size we forecast still leaves operating profit above the prior year, and why the earnings are more cyclical than the EBITDA line [S4].

Depreciation needs a correction before any of this is comparable. The data pack carries depreciation for FY2025 that is only the general and administration allocation, while the audited fixed-asset note shows total depreciation of IDR19.7bn, with the difference sitting in cost of goods sold [S4, F1, F2]. We restate the full amount in our forecast, which is why our depreciation ratio is higher than the pack's and why our EBITDA margin is lower than a pack-based calculation would suggest [S4, F1, F2]. The restatement does not change operating profit, cash flow or the valuation, but it does change every EBITDA multiple in this report [S4].

Working capital is the balance-sheet story. The company prepays for molasses at the harvest, so operating working capital is structurally large relative to sales rather than a sign of distress [S6]. At the end of September 2026 advances for purchases stood at IDR152.9bn against a much smaller balance at the start of the year, funded by short-term bank loans of IDR86.6bn [S6, F22, F23]. The prepayment converts into inventory and then into cost of goods sold over the following quarters, so the revolver balance is a seasonal funding line rather than a permanent capital need [S6].

Cash conversion is not a durable trait; it is the harvest cycle. The audited record is a negative FY2024 operating cash flow in the same statement that shows the FY2025 figure, and FY2025's IDR255.8bn against net profit of IDR77.4bn is mostly a working-capital release of IDR-147.9bn as the prior year's prepayment unwound [S4, F33]. The first half of 2026 then generated IDR128.9bn and the nine months only IDR30.2bn, so the third quarter consumed about IDR128.9bn less IDR30.2bn as the harvest prepayment went out, against nine-month net profit of roughly a hundred billion rupiah [S5, S6, F34, F36]. Capital expenditure was IDR35.0bn in FY2025 and almost nothing in the first nine months of 2026, so the cash is real, but it arrives in the fourth quarter and it reverses in the third: a reader should not capitalise one good year of conversion [S4, S6, F17]. The company is not investing for growth: the acetic acid and ethyl acetate plants are idle and no expansion has been announced [S3, F28].

The dividend is a fixed rupiah amount rather than a payout ratio. The company paid IDR6.6bn in 2026, roughly a rupiah a share against earnings per share of Rp13, and it has paid a flat rupiah dividend in most years since listing, with one larger payment and one year of no dividend in the record [S3, S6, F27]. We therefore model the flat rupiah amount the record supports rather than a payout policy the company has never stated: the payout ratio falls as earnings rise so that DPS stays near the observed level, and the target roll-forward subtracts the IDR6.6bn the record implies rather than a percentage of a peak year's profit [S4, S6, F27].

Three earnings-quality flags deserve mention. First, other income is not trivial: FY2025 included a foreign-exchange gain, an insurance claim and a gain on asset sales, partly offset by an impairment of trade receivables, and the nine months of 2026 again include a large other-income line [S4, S6]. We carry only the recurring element in our forecast and exclude the one-offs [S4]. Second, the company bought land in FY2024 from three directors and a family member at a price disclosed in the related-party note, a transaction that is small relative to assets but is exactly the kind of dealing a minority holder should price [S4]. Third, the pack's depreciation understatement, corrected above, is a reminder that the vendor data for this name is not clean [S4, F1].

Our forecast is deliberately unheroic on margin and modest on volume. We assume revenue falls -7.0% in FY2026E because nine months were below the prior year and the fourth quarter is carried at the third-quarter run-rate (the board's own IDR950.0bn projection for 2026 is not a ceiling: nine-month sales of IDR862.9bn already passed it), then grows in the low single digits as volume recovers toward capacity and the blend mandate adds domestic demand [S6, S8, S9]. Gross margin fades from 29.7% to 24.5% as the competitive spread on industrial, food-grade and export volumes narrows, and operating costs grow slower than sales [S3, S4, F28]. The fade is not sourced to the molasses formula, and the report should say so plainly: the ministry's HIP passes molasses through one-for-one and fixes the fuel-grade spread in dollars, so it can neither explain the 2026 windfall nor produce its fade; the template carries no molasses price variable, so the fade is a margin path and a judgement about supply response in the unpriced volumes [S10, F25, F26]. The FY2026E EBITDA margin of 16.1% against the 11.1% actual is the same gross-margin step, not a new operating-leverage assumption: the nine months of 2026 already printed an EBITDA margin above seventeen per cent on the existing fixed cost base [S6]. Net profit is IDR122.6bn in FY2026E and IDR95.9bn in FY2030E, and earnings per share fall from Rp20 to Rp16 as the margin normalises [S4].

We value Indo Acidatama on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a P/E cross-check. The mix fits a single-asset converter with a finite capacity, a contracted feedstock and a policy-set price on part of its output: the cash flow is forecastable, the asset has no reserve life to model, and the terminal value is a plant-life perpetuity rather than a depleting resource [S3]. The two multiples are there to test whether the market's own pricing of comparable chemical assets agrees with the cash flow, and on the peak year they broadly do, with the procyclical caveat set out below [S4].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck, not from the accounts. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesian country premium 2.5% (macro deck); the beta of 0.92 is the chemicals industry default in the house configuration, levered at the June net-cash capital structure, and is one of the two unsourced inputs in the build — we state it as a default rather than dress it as a peer estimate. The second is the 1.6% sovereign default spread the house deducts from the rupiah risk-free rate before adding the beta-weighted premia, a cost-of-capital convention rather than a sourced input. So the cost of equity is 7.4% less 1.6% plus 0.92 times the sum of the mature-market and country premia, 12.0%, and the weighted average cost of capital is 11.9% [S4]. The balance sheet is almost all equity at the valuation date, so the cost of equity is effectively the whole discount rate and a one-point change in it moves value by roughly the amount the discount-rate sensitivity below shows. We use a terminal growth rate set at long-run rupiah inflation rather than at nominal output growth, because the plant is capacity-bound and real volume growth in perpetuity is not creditable [S3].

The cash flow forecast runs from the June 2026 balance sheet, which is the data pack's valuation date. The first forecast year is counted from the first of July, so the stub is about half a year, and we replace the even proration with the second-half flow the actual cash flow implies. The first half of 2026 generated operating cash flow of IDR128.9bn and the nine months only IDR30.2bn, so the third quarter was a working-capital build of about IDR128.9bn less IDR30.2bn as the harvest prepayment went out; the fourth quarter is the unwind, and the fourth quarter of 2025 alone delivered the difference between the full year and the nine months [S5, S6, F34, F36]. Struck like-for-like, the bridge is unlevered on both sides: first-half operating cash flow plus back the after-tax interest paid covers about half as much again as the evenly prorated full-year stub the engine would otherwise discount, so the second-half stub is cut by somewhat more than half [S5, S6]. The correction is a timing item, not a balance-sheet item, and it costs about eight rupiah a share of equity value; because the engine applies one bridge scalar it also lands on the EV/EBITDA and P/E legs, where a half-year cash-flow timing item means nothing, worth about three rupiah of the blended value. That is an engine limitation we cannot remove from the assumptions file, and we would rather disclose it than hide it [S5, S6].

The discounted cash flow gives Rp152 a share, with the terminal value at 39.3% of the total, which is low for a perpetuity-based model and reflects the near-term cash generation rather than a distant terminal assumption [S4]. The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp154 a share on 5.5 times our FY2026E EBITDA, and the P/E cross-check gives Rp172 on 8.3 times our FY2026E earnings [S4]. The EV/EBITDA leg is within a couple of per cent of the primary and the P/E leg is about a seventh above it, which is the expected pattern for a company whose earnings are more cyclical than its EBITDA because of the fixed cost base [S4].

The agreement across methods is narrower than it looks, and we should be explicit about why. Both multiples are applied to FY2026E, the peak year: the EBITDA leg is 5.5 times peak EBITDA and the P/E leg 8.3 times peak earnings. That is procyclical, and it is the one place where the house weights put forty per cent of the value on a year we ourselves call a spike. Applied instead to FY2028E, when the margin has faded to 27.0%, the P/E leg falls to roughly the discounted cash flow, so the peak-year basis is an upper bound rather than independent corroboration [S4]. The through-cycle markers are: a normalised gross margin of 24.5%, which is the top of the pre-2025 range rather than the peak; net debt at the September reporting date of the order of IDR86.6bn less IDR18.6bn against FY2024 trough EBITDA of IDR58.6bn, about one and a fifth times; and a dividend-capacity yield on the current share price that the flat rupiah dividend sets well below a bond. We keep the house weights of sixty per cent discounted cash flow, twenty-five per cent EV/EBITDA and fifteen per cent P/E because the DCF is the method that actually fades the margin, and the blend is Rp155 a share before the roll-forward to the target [S4, S6, F20, F22].

The sensitivity grid shows what has to be true for the shares to be worth today's price, within the range it actually tests. Moving the discount rate up one percentage point and terminal growth down one still leaves the discounted cash flow above Rp100, at the lowest corner of the discount-rate grid; the grid does not run a two-point discount-rate shock, and we do not claim it does [S4]. The growth and margin grid is the more instructive one and it does not reach the price either: even at four points off our growth rate and two points off the margin, the value stays above Rp100, so the grid's axes stop short of the market's implicit bet [S4]. That bet is not slower growth. It is a permanent reversal of the molasses spread, and the scenario that tests it is the bear case below, which takes the gross margin to the FY2024 trough and prints Rp84 [S4].

The reverse discounted cash flow makes the same point from the other direction. The engine cannot solve for a revenue growth rate that justifies the current price and reports the price as outside the bracket rather than returning a number, so the price is not a growth call at all [S4]. What the price does imply is a margin call. At Rp100 the market capitalisation is IDR602,000,000,000.0bn against our FY2026E net profit of IDR122.6bn and book value per share of Rp154 [S4, S6]. That book value is not the book a minority holder is buying: IDR165.3bn of it is a PSAK 16 revaluation surplus on land and buildings, so pre-revaluation book is about a fifth below the reported Rp154, and the shares trade at about four-fifths of that pre-revaluation book rather than the two-thirds the headline suggests, for a business earning a mid-teens return on the reported equity and a higher return on the pre-revaluation one [S6, F37, S4]. Either the market expects the return on equity to halve, or it is charging a governance and float discount that our cash flow does not capture [S3, S4].

We do not apply a liquidity discount. Three-month average daily traded value is IDR29,514,784,112.7bn, which is above the house floor at which a discount would be required, and the free float of 31.9% is above the exchange minimum [S3]. The float is small in absolute terms and the family can move the register, which is a real risk discussed in the next section, but it is not a liquidity discount in the mechanical sense [S3].

The first risk is the molasses price, and it is a two-sided risk rather than a pure downside. A poor cane harvest raises the input cost, and because the regulated reference price is a trailing three-month average, the company is under-compensated for a rapid move before the formula catches up [S10, F26]. A good harvest does the opposite and is what produced the current margin [S3, S4]. The company's own outlook names dependence on the agricultural and sugar sectors as a supply risk, and it holds contracts for only about a year of requirements at a time [S3, F14].

The second risk is policy. The blend mandate is the main source of new domestic demand, but the first allocation went to three producers with a combined capacity the ministry describes as small, and Indo Acidatama is not named among them [S9]. If the company is excluded from the fuel-grade allocation, the mandate is a demand signal for its competitors rather than for it, and the volume growth we credit in FY2027E and beyond would not arrive [S9, S11]. The mandate could also slip: the ten per cent blend has been announced for 2027 but the technical rules and the feedstock commitment were still being prepared when the minister spoke [S11].

The third risk is the working-capital cycle. The harvest prepayment is funded by short-term bank loans, and at the end of September 2026 those loans were IDR86.6bn against cash of IDR18.6bn [S6, F20, F22]. If the molasses is not delivered on schedule, or if the company prepays more than it can convert, the revolver stays drawn into the following year and the interest cost rises [S6]. That is net debt of about IDR86.6bn less IDR18.6bn at the reporting date, not net cash: we define net debt as loans less cash and do not net the purchase advances against it, because those advances are an operating asset already inside the working-capital ratio and netting them would count them twice [S6, F20, F22, F23]. The company has managed this cycle for years, but it is the reason the reported net cash position is not a stable number, and the reason we do not claim the balance sheet is debt-free [S6, F23].

The fourth risk is governance and the float. Insider holdings are 65.9% and the free float is 31.9%, so a small number of family holders control the company and the traded register is thin [S3]. The FY2024 land purchases from directors and a family member show that related-party dealings are part of how the controlling group operates, even when they are small [S4]. A minority holder is relying on the family to keep paying the dividend and not to redirect value through related-party transactions [S3, S4].

The fifth risk is the export book and the currency. About a third of ethanol revenue is exported and priced in dollars, so a stronger rupiah hurts realisations, while the company's dollar costs are limited to imported freight and some raw materials [S4, F7, F11]. The company itself flags a stronger dollar and higher funding costs as 2026 pressures, which is the opposite direction, but the exposure cuts both ways [S3].

Our bear case is a trough-margin path, not a haircut: the gross margin returns to the FY2024 trough of 16.6%, a poor harvest lifts molasses and trims output, a coal cost shock lands on a plant that takes nine tenths of its energy from coal, the company is left out of the fuel allocation, the ten per cent blend slips, and the harvest prepayment does not unwind so the revolver stays drawn [S3, S6, S9, S10]. It is worth Rp84 a share, below today's price, so the market is pricing something between our trough and our base rather than a growth disappointment [S4]. Our bull case assumes the company is named in the allocation, the blend accelerates, the harvest is good and the idle acetic acid plant restarts; it is worth Rp248 [S7, S9, S11]. The base case, at Rp173, carries half the weight [S4]. The asymmetry is deliberate and should be read: the bull adds about four tenths to the base value while the bear takes away more than half of it, because the upside is capped by a formula-fixed fuel-grade spread and the downside is not capped at all [S10, F26].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A monthly reference price that stops rising while molasses keeps rising would tell us the formula is lagging and the spread is compressing [S10]. A producer list that excludes the company would remove the volume leg of the bull case [S9]. A first-half result with a gross margin back near the FY2024 level would say the current margin was a one-quarter event rather than a cycle [S4]. And a related-party transaction larger than the dividend would change the governance discount from a nuisance to a valuation input [S4].

The company is controlled by the Setijo and Budhi families through direct holdings and three family companies, and the president director is a member of the Budhi family [S3]. Local individuals held 61.1% of the shares at the end of FY2025, local companies held most of the rest, and foreign ownership was negligible [S3, F29]. Insider holdings of 65.9% and a free float of 31.9% mean the shares are liquid enough to trade but not liquid enough for most institutional mandates [S3].

The board is family-dominated but not unprofessional. The directors include an independent director who is also the finance and administration director, a plant director, an administration director and a business development director from the Setijo family, and the company has an audit committee, an internal audit function and a corporate secretary [S3]. The FY2025 accounts were audited by a firm in the RSM network with an unmodified opinion, which is the minimum standard and is met [S3].

Related-party dealings are disclosed and small in aggregate but not absent. Sales to a company under common control and to a sister textile company were a fraction of a per cent of revenue in FY2025, and receivables from those parties were similarly small [S4]. The larger item is the FY2024 purchase of land from three directors and a family member, which is a related-party asset purchase at a valuation the minority cannot independently test [S4]. We treat this as a governance discount rather than a red flag, but it is the reason we do not argue for a re-rating to book [S4].

The dividend record is the main protection for a minority holder. The company has paid a flat rupiah dividend in most years since listing, skipped one year, paid a larger amount once, and raised the payment in 2026 to IDR6.6bn in total [S3, F27]. With a payout in the high single digits of profit the dividend is not a yield story, but it is a cash return that has survived a full commodity cycle [S3, S4].

On ESG, the company's main exposure is energy and emissions. Its 2025 energy consumption was dominated by coal, with purchased electricity a distant second and diesel a rounding error, and its emissions intensity per tonne of production rose over the three years disclosed [S3]. The company says it uses methane from its own waste treatment as a boiler fuel to reduce fossil fuel use, which is a genuine abatement measure rather than a disclosure exercise [S3]. Water and effluent are the other exposure: the plant discharges into the surrounding area and reports biological oxygen demand and suspended solids in its sustainability table [S3]. There were no reported corruption incidents in the period covered by the report [S3].

The free float is the governance issue that could resolve itself. At 31.9% the company is above the exchange's minimum but below the level at which it would enter most indices, and the exchange has been tightening the rules for concentrated-ownership names [S3]. A family sell-down would improve liquidity and index eligibility, and it is the single event most likely to close the valuation gap without any change in the business [S3].

The dated catalysts are the results calendar and the policy calendar. Full-year results in the first quarter of 2027 will be the first clean read on whether the molasses spread held through the fourth quarter, when the harvest prepayment is at its peak [S6]. The implementation of the ten per cent blend, announced for 2027, will determine whether the volume leg of our forecast arrives [S11]. The monthly reference price is the highest-frequency marker of the domestic fuel-grade spread and is published by the energy ministry [S10]. The annual meeting will set the dividend for the year [S3].

Between updates we monitor four numbers. The monthly bioethanol reference price against the molasses benchmark tells us whether the formula is compensating or lagging [S10, F24, F25]. Ethanol production against the 78,825 kilolitre capacity tells us whether volume is growing without new capital [S3, F5]. The advances for purchases and the short-term bank loan balance tell us whether the harvest cycle is unwinding on schedule [S6, F22, F23]. And the gross margin tells us whether the current spread is a cycle or a quarter [S4, S6].

bear.narrative: A trough-margin path, not a haircut: the molasses spread gives back the whole 2026 windfall and the gross margin returns to the FY2024 trough of 16.6%, which is the path section 4 shows the market price implies. A poor cane harvest lifts molasses, a quarter of output is lost to feedstock shortage, SRSN is left out of the E5 allocation because it is not one of the three named producers, and E10 slips past 2028. Coal at 90.2% of energy consumed makes a coal cost shock a second squeeze. Industrial and export ethanol realisations fall with regional oversupply, the acetic acid plant stays idle, the harvest prepayment does not unwind on schedule so the revolver stays drawn at the September level of IDR86.6bn, and the dividend is held at Rp1.1 rather than raised [S3, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10].

bull.narrative: SRSN is named among the producers allocated volume under the E5 mandate, and the earlier E10 start pulls fuel-grade ethanol through the system; the 8% capacity headroom is filled. A strong cane harvest keeps molasses near Rp1,816/kg while the HIP formula lifts the reference price with the rupiah, food-grade and export prices hold with regional stocks low, and the acetic acid plant restarts at a positive spread. The harvest prepayment unwinds faster than the base, freeing the revolver, and the family raises the dividend [S3, S7, S8, S9, S10].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -7.0% is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate. 9M2026 net sales were IDR862.9bn (Q1 IDR239.5bn, Q2 IDR318.1bn, Q3 IDR305.3bn) against 9M2025 IDR953.1bn, down 9.5% year on year [S6, F18]. The fourth-quarter 2025 base is IDR303.3bn, the audited FY2025 net sales of IDR1,256.4bn less 9M2025; a fourth quarter at the Q3 level gives about IDR305bn, so FY2026E revenue is IDR1,168bn [S3, S4]. The board's own 2026 projection of IDR950bn is not a constraint on this: it was written before the molasses spread widened and nine-month sales of IDR862.9bn have already exceeded it, so the plan is stale rather than a ceiling [S3, S6, F31]. FY2027E +3.5% and FY2028E +4.5% rest on volume, not price: installed ethanol capacity is 78,825kl against 73,029kl produced in FY2025, so 92.6% utilisation leaves about 8% headroom, and the E5 mandate began in July 2026 but covers only Java, uses domestic feedstock and names just three eligible producers with 26,000kl of combined capacity, and SRSN is not confirmed as one of them [S3, F5, F3, S8, S9]. We do NOT capitalise the 400,000-500,000kl national E20 requirement as SRSN volume: national feedstock is only about 70,500kl and the government expects 11 new plants, so the mandate is a demand tailwind, not a volume guarantee [S7, S9]. FY2029E +4.0% and FY2030E +3.5% taper toward nominal GDP; the 3.0% long run is the deck's rupiah inflation and sits below the IDR terminal cap.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 29.7% blends the nine-month actual with a softer fourth quarter. The nine months earned gross profit of IDR260.2bn on net sales of IDR862.9bn, a 30.2% margin, against 22.7% for 9M2025 [S6]. The fourth quarter is carried at about 28.5%, giving roughly IDR347bn of full-year gross profit, because the November 2026 HIP puts molasses at Rp1,816/kg in its formula, so the input cost base that the fourth quarter will be charged against is known and higher than the average that produced the first nine months [S10, F25]. The fade to 24.5% by FY2030E and 24.0% long run is a competitive-margin judgement on the volumes that actually earned the 2026 spread, NOT a pass-through mechanism: the HIP formula only prices fuel-grade ethanol, and section 2 states that the margin was earned on industrial, food-grade and export volumes where the ministry formula does not set the price [S3, S10, F26]. There is no molasses price variable in this template, so the fade is not a mirrored feedstock path; it is the judgement that the FY2025-FY2026 spread is a wide point in a competitive market with no product-mix protection (the acetic acid and ethyl acetate plants did not operate in 2025), and that it gives back part of the excess as domestic and Brazilian/Chinese supply responds [S3, S4, F28]. The 30.2% nine-month margin is above the whole FY2022-FY2025 range of 16.6% to 24.8%, so we stop the fade at the top of that range rather than at the trough [S4]. FY2027E 28.5%, FY2028E 27.0%, FY2029E 25.5%, FY2030E 24.5%. The fade is the largest single value driver at roughly Rp12 a share per point of gross margin, which the sensitivity grid shows.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Set to zero: the 2025 sustainability table records coal at 781,809.54 GJ of 866,313.67 GJ consumed (90.2%), purchased electricity at 83,263.23 GJ (9.6%) and diesel at only 1,240.90 GJ (0.14%), so Brent prices essentially none of the production cost [S3]. The only oil exposure is diesel inside freight, which the accounts fold into selling and distribution and do not separate. We therefore do not carry an oil link rather than invent a share; the P&L is a molasses-cost business [S3, S10].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set to zero with the share: with no disclosed oil-linked cost there is no pass-through to estimate. The regulated bioethanol HIP is indexed to molasses, not Brent, and about a third of ethanol revenue is exported (IDR380.6bn of IDR1,066.0bn in FY2025), where prices are set in the regional market [S10, S4, F7, F11].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling expenses of IDR125.6bn plus general and administration of IDR66.1bn total IDR191.7bn, 15.3% of revenue; the nine months to September 2026 ran at 15.4% (operating expenses IDR133.0bn on sales of IDR862.9bn) [S4, S6]. We hold 15.4% and let it drift to 14.8% as the overhead base grows slower than revenue once the molasses price effect annualises [S4, S6].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation is restated from the fixed-asset note, not the data pack: FY2025 total D&A was IDR19.721817bn, of which IDR15.002383bn sits in cost of goods sold and IDR4.719434bn in general and administration, while the pack carries only the SG&A share [S4, F1, F2]. On FY2025 revenue of IDR1,256.4bn that is 1.57%; the nine months of 2026 charged IDR15.649bn of depreciation on IDR862.9bn, 1.81%, so we hold 1.8% and ease to 1.7% [S6].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 acquisition of fixed assets was IDR35.0bn (2.8% of revenue) and FY2024 IDR60.2bn (5.2%), but nine-month 2026 capex was only IDR0.7bn against IDR33.1bn in the same period of 2025 [S4, S6, F17]. The plant is capacity-bound on molasses rather than on equipment, no expansion is announced, and the two idle plants (acetic acid, ethyl acetate) are not being restarted, so we hold capex at 2.0% of revenue, close to the restated D&A ratio of 1.7-1.8% plus routine replacement [S3, S4, F28].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was 41.3% of revenue in FY2025 (IDR519.0bn), 57.8% in FY2024 and 51.0% in FY2023 [S0]. The high level is structural: molasses is bought against the cane harvest and advances for purchases reached IDR152.9bn at 30 September 2026 against IDR66.9bn at end-2025, a seasonal prepayment that unwinds as the molasses is delivered and crushed [S6, F23]. We hold 41% rather than the pack's three-year 50%, which double counts the harvest peak [S0, S6].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax expense was IDR23.3bn on pre-tax profit of IDR100.6bn, 23.1%, and the nine months of 2026 ran at 22.1% (IDR28.5bn on IDR128.7bn) [S4, S6]. We hold 22.5%, the statutory 22% plus a small permanent-difference drag, through the forecast [S6].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense of IDR20.3bn on average debt of about IDR212bn is 9.6%; the nine months of 2026 charged IDR3.1bn against a much smaller average loan balance because the revolver was undrawn until the third quarter [S4, S6]. We hold 9.5%, the effective rate on the working-capital facilities with Bank Central Asia [S6].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income was IDR7.6m on opening cash of IDR4.7bn, 0.16%, because the balance is held in current accounts for the molasses payment cycle rather than invested [S4]. We hold 0.2% [S4].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No term debt is issued in the forecast: the company funds the harvest with a revolving working-capital facility that is repaid inside the year, so the opening balance sheet's net cash position is carried and the seasonal swing is captured in working capital [S6].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Other income net of other expenses was IDR1.9bn in FY2025 (FX gain IDR3.8bn and insurance claim IDR1.9bn against a IDR4.8bn receivable impairment) and IDR4.6bn in the nine months of 2026 [S4, S6]. We carry IDR1.5bn, the recurring FX-gain element, and exclude the one-off impairment and insurance claim [S4].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interest: the balance sheet carries no non-controlling interest at 30 June 2026 or 30 September 2026 [S0, S6].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The record is a flat rupiah amount, not a payout ratio: Rp1.0 a share for FY2022-FY2024 and Rp1.1 for FY2025 (IDR6.622bn on 6,020m shares), paid through an earnings swing from IDR22.5bn to IDR77.4bn [S3, S0, F27]. We therefore model the flat rupiah amount the record supports, and let the payout ratio fall as earnings rise: payout is set so that DPS stays near Rp1.1 a share (5.4% of FY2026E EPS of 20.36, easing to 6.9% by FY2030E as EPS falls back). The company has never stated a payout policy, so we do not assume one [S3].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No share issuance or buyback: 6,020,000,000 shares outstanding at 30 September 2026, unchanged from the prior year, and no dilutive instruments [S6].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0% nominal, deliberately below the macro deck's FY2027E rupiah inflation of 3.28% and far below nominal GDP, rather than at either: the plant is a capacity-bound single site whose ethanol volume is limited by molasses supply rather than by equipment, so real volume growth in perpetuity is not creditable, while prices and costs escalate with inflation. The 2.0% maintenance capex ratio is consistent with no real growth capex, and 3.0% sits below the 5% IDR terminal cap [S3, S6].

challenges.challenge: The ministry capacity quote is misattributed: the source says 26,000 kl, the report says 78,825 kl, which is SRSN's own capacity.
challenges.answer: The ministry figure is 26,000 kl: S9 states "berkisar di angka 26 ribu kiloliter (KL)" for the three cleared producers, and 78,825 kl is SRSN's own capacity from the annual report capacity table. Added F35 keyed to that quote; section 2 now prints F35 for the ministry and F5 for the company and says the company's capacity is a third of nothing but three times the cleared pool, so the section 5 inference (SRSN is not one of the three) is strengthened, not weakened, and the self-contradiction is gone.

challenges.challenge: IDR128.9bn is the six-month operating cash flow from the S5 interim filing, not the nine-month figure; the Q3 filing shows IDR111.6bn, and F34 is labelled 2026Q3 against a six-month source.
challenges.answer: FATAL accepted: F34 is the six-month figure (S5 is headed "For the Six Month Period Ended 30 Juni 2026"), not 2026Q3, and the report wrongly called it nine months. The proposed replacement figure is itself wrong: in the S6 cash-flow statement the columns are 1 Jan-30 Sep 2026 and 1 Jan-30 Sep 2025, and 111.628bn is the 2025 comparative; the nine-month 2026 figure is 30.224bn, corroborated by cash capex of 0.700bn and closing cash of 18.599bn in the same column. Added F36 for 9M2026. The bridge itself survives on a like-for-like unlevered basis: H1 operating cash flow 128.9 plus back after-tax interest gives ~130.6 of H1 unlevered FCF, so the full-year FCFF of 167.1 leaves ~36.5 for H2 against the 84.2 prorated stub, about -47.7, which is the -47.5 the file carries. Section 3 now states the H1 to 9M swing and its meaning.

challenges.challenge: The claim of three years of strong cash conversion is contradicted by FY2024 operating cash flow of minus IDR99.2bn, which sits in the same cash-flow statement.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 3 and thesis bullet 4 no longer claim three years of strong conversion. FY2024 operating cash flow was negative in the same audited statement that shows the FY2025 figure, and the report now says FY2025's 255.8bn is mostly the 147.9bn working-capital release (model delta_nwc FY2025A), then shows the 9M2026 figure of 30.2bn against nine-month net profit of 100.2bn. The paragraph draws the conclusion the card requires: do not capitalise one good year of conversion.

challenges.challenge: The drift.gross_margin justification explains the fade through the HIP pass-through, but the report itself says the margin is earned on industrial, food-grade and export volumes that the formula does not price, and the model contains no molasses price path.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the mechanism, rebutted on the number. There is no molasses variable in the template and no sourced path that produces the fade, so the fade is now stated as a competitive-margin judgement on the industrial, food-grade and export volumes, explicitly NOT sourced to HIP: the report says the formula passes molasses through one-for-one and fixes the fuel-grade spread, so it can neither explain the 2026 windfall nor produce the fade. The evidence for the fade is that 30.2% sits above the whole FY2022-FY2025 range and the idle acetic acid and ethyl acetate plants leave no specialty mix to defend it; we stop at the top of the historical range, not at the trough. The QC justification and the assumption basis both say this now.

challenges.challenge: The shares are called below book at Rp154 without removing the IDR165.3bn revaluation surplus that the earnings-quality card requires to be stripped from any price-to-book work.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added F37 for the 165.3bn PSAK 16 revaluation surplus from the S6 equity statement (Other Equity Components), and sections 4, the investment summary and the extreme_call justification now present pre-revaluation book. The below-book argument survives but is weaker and the report says so: at about four-fifths of pre-revaluation book the shares are still below it, but the discount is smaller than the headline two-thirds, and ROE on pre-revaluation equity is higher than the reported figure. The 0.69x line is gone.

challenges.challenge: EV/EBITDA and P/E are both applied to FY2026E peak earnings for 40% of the value, and no through-cycle marker is stated anywhere in the report.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now says plainly that both multiples capitalise FY2026E, that this is procyclical and is the weakest part of the weight, and that applied to FY2028E at the faded margin the P/E leg falls to roughly the DCF, so the peak-year basis is an upper bound rather than corroboration. It states the through-cycle markers the card requires: the normalising gross margin (FY2030E, top of the pre-2025 range), net debt at the reporting date against FY2024 trough EBITDA of 58.6 (about 1.2x), and a dividend-capacity yield below a bond. We keep the house 60/25/15 weights because the DCF is the only method that fades the margin, and say that is the reason.

challenges.challenge: The minus IDR47.5bn bridge subtracts an after-interest, after-tax operating cash flow from an unlevered FCFF stub and is then applied to the EV/EBITDA and P/E legs, which do not carry period cash flow.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the definition, rebutted on the size. The bridge is now struck unlevered on both sides: first-half operating cash flow plus back the after-tax interest paid (2.4bn) against the unlevered full-year FCFF, which reproduces about -47.7 and confirms the -47.5 in the file. The section 3 and 4 text no longer describes the input as nine months. On applying it to the multiple legs we cannot comply: the engine applies one bridge scalar to all three methods, we cannot edit the engine or model, and section 4 therefore discloses it and quantifies it at about three rupiah of the blended value against eight rupiah on the DCF leg.

challenges.challenge: The report says the company carries no net debt once advances are netted against the revolver, but the latest balance sheet shows IDR68.0bn of net debt and the model's net debt line uses a different cash-flow base from the DCF.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The "no net debt" claim is gone from the summary, thesis bullet 3, section 5 and the extreme_call justification. Net debt is now defined as short-term bank loans less cash, 86.603bn less 18.599bn, IDR68.0bn at 30 September 2026, with a stated reason for not netting the advances (they are an operating asset already inside the 41% working-capital ratio and netting them would double count). The report explains that the DCF starts on the June balance sheet with 17.9bn of net cash and that the model's own year-end FY2026E net cash of 49.9bn is the same seasonal unwind, not a different cash-flow base hidden from the reader.

challenges.challenge: The bear case at Rp124 sits above the market price and only removes 4pp of margin, yet section 4 argues the market is pricing a permanent return to the FY2024 trough margin of 16.6%.
challenges.answer: Accepted and taken into the numbers. The bear gross-margin shock is now -8pp rather than -4pp, so the bear returns the margin to the FY2024 trough and prints below the price (83.73) instead of 124.46. The bear narrative names the trough margin, the harvest loss, the coal cost shock on a 90.2% coal energy base and the revolver staying drawn. The investment summary no longer claims the price is below the bear: it sits between the bear and the base, which is the honest read. The outcome asymmetry is stated (bull about +43% on base, bear about -52%) and attributed to the formula-capped upside. The sensitivity grid is now described within its tested range, and the report says the grid's axes stop short of the market price and that the bear scenario is the test that brackets it.

challenges.challenge: The 36.6kt acetic acid plant and the ethyl acetate line produced nothing in FY2025 and carry neither a valuation nor an impairment review, although the bull narrative depends on a restart.
challenges.answer: Partly accepted. Section 1 now states that the 36.6kt acetic acid line stays inside the fixed-asset block with no separate impairment recognised in FY2025 or in the nine months of 2026 and no impairment test disclosed, that the base case gives it no earnings but does not write it down, so its carrying value is tested in the price-to-book cross-check rather than in the cash flow, and that a restart is a revenue event, which is why the bull carries a revenue shock and not a margin one. We cannot size tonnes times a sourced acetic acid price because the pack has no acetic acid price series (the FY2025 traded acid segment revenue of 89.65bn has no disclosed volume), and we will not invent one; the bull's revenue shock is where the restart sits.

challenges.challenge: 124kt of contracted molasses cannot cover a full year of 73,029kl of ethanol output at the 4.125 kg/litre conversion the report itself relies on.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The "full year of production" claim is deleted. Section 1 now converts the 124kt at the 4.125 kg/litre in the ministry formula, which supports about thirty thousand kilolitres against the 73,029kl produced, so the contracts cover roughly two-fifths of requirements and the balance is bought from the 29 suppliers. The paragraph draws both consequences: the moat is narrower than a headline contract implies, and the cost model cannot be a contracted-price model. The 4.125 factor is the ministry formula's, not a company yield, and the report says so.

challenges.challenge: The report calls the dividend a fixed rupiah amount and then models 8.6% of profit, raising DPS by 59% and feeding it into the target.
challenges.answer: Accepted. We model the flat rupiah amount: the payout ratio now falls from 5.4% to 6.9% across the forecast so that DPS stays near Rp1.1 a share, and dps12 in the target roll-forward is Rp1.10 rather than the Rp1.75 the old 8.6% path produced, which is why the target moved. Section 3 says the payout ratio falls as earnings rise and that we do not assume a policy the company has never stated.

challenges.challenge: The text says moving the discount rate up two percentage points still leaves the DCF above the price, but the grid steps WACC by plus or minus one point.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The sentence now says one percentage point, not two, and cites the lowest corner of the discount-rate grid; it says explicitly that the grid does not run a two-point shock and that we do not claim it does. We did not extend the axis because the sensitivity grid is engine-generated and we do not edit the engine.

challenges.challenge: The one-fifth-of-growth reverse-DCF result is not produced by the engine, which reports only that the price is not bracketed, and it is cited to a financial statement.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The "fifth of our growth rate" specific is deleted. Section 4 now reports what the engine actually returns: no growth rate brackets the price, the block reports the price as outside the bracket, and the growth and margin grid taken to four points off growth and two off margin still discounts above the price. The citation is the model and its sensitivity table, not a financial statement.

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity and WACC are cited to S4, the FY2025 audited accounts, while the beta is an unsourced industry default.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now attributes the risk-free rate, mature-market premium and country premium to the house macro deck and states that the beta is the chemicals industry default in the house configuration, levered at the June capital structure, and calls it the one unsourced input rather than dressing it as a peer estimate. It notes that with an almost all-equity balance sheet the cost of equity is effectively the whole discount rate and points to the discount-rate sensitivity for the one-point effect. missing_bull_case.note: Two upsides are absent from value. missing_bear_case.note: The bear case is milder than the scenario the report says the market is pricing. valuation_method_fit.note: DCF-FCFF as primary is right for a single-asset converter with no reserve life, and terminal growth set at inflation is defensible. But forty per cent of the weight sits on FY2026E, the peak year, which the commodity-cyclical card names procyclical error number one, and the card's output contract (through-cycle price named, cost-curve quartile, dividend-capacity yield, net-debt to trough-EBITDA) is not delivered. The price-to-book argument uses post-revaluation book although equity carries an IDR165.3bn PSAK 16 revaluation surplus. The minus IDR47.5bn DCF timing bridge is applied as a scalar to the multiple legs and mixes unlevered FCFF with an after-interest, after-tax operating cash flow.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is candid about the bear side: the margin is called a spike, SRSN is said not to be confirmed in the allocation, the governance discount is named, and the bull case is not presented as the point estimate. The rating is not driven by one heroic input because the base margin fades every year of the forecast. consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The link is set to the oil deck with a zero share, which is honest given coal is 90.2% of energy and molasses is the swing cost, but no coal driver substitutes for it even though the energy mix is cited in the same paragraph. conservatism_audit.note: Cautious-side departures without a source: the 41% NWC ratio (lowest of three years), terminal growth held at 3.0% below both the deck inflation and nominal-GDP paths even though the mandate is a volume tailwind, and the minus IDR47.5bn bridge that lowers all three methods. flags.message: a.gross_margin moves -5.7pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The 5.2pp fall from 29.7% in FY2026E to 24.5% in FY2030E is a competitive-margin judgement, not a feed-through mechanism. Section 2 establishes that the margin was earned on industrial, food-grade and export volumes where prices are set by competition; the HIP formula prices only fuel-grade ethanol and passes molasses through one-for-one, so it cannot explain either the 2026 windfall or its fade [S3, S10, F26]. The 30.2% nine-month margin sits above the whole FY2022-FY2025 range of 16.6% to 24.8%, and with the acetic acid and ethyl acetate plants idle there is no specialty mix to defend it [S3, S4, F28]. The fade stops at 24.0% long run, above the FY2024 trough, so it is a reversion to the top of the historical range rather than a bear case; the bear scenario takes the margin to the trough itself. The template has no molasses price variable, so the fade is carried as a margin path and the report says so.

flags.message: a.gross_margin: bear -0.08 vs bull 0.04 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The bear is deliberately deeper than the bull is higher, and the asymmetry is sourced. The FY2024 trough gross margin of 16.6% is a realised audited outcome, so a return to it is a documented downside path, not a stress [S4]. The upside is capped: the HIP formula fixes the fuel-grade spread at a flat US dollar margin and passes molasses through one-for-one, so a better feedstock year cannot lift the regulated leg, and the plant already runs at 92.6% of installed capacity, so the bull's upside is volume and mix rather than a wider spread [S10, F26, F5, F3].

flags.message: a.payout: bear +0 and bull +0.02 do not point opposite ways
flags.justification: The dividend is a flat rupiah amount rather than a payout ratio, so the bear holds it at Rp1.1 a share (a zero shock) instead of cutting it, and the bull raises it. A cut is not in the record: the company has skipped the dividend once since listing and paid a flat Rp1.0-1.1 through an earnings swing from IDR22.5bn to IDR77.4bn, so a cut would be a governance event we do not put in the base bear [S3, S0, F27].

flags.message: expected return +70%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is the gap between a 4.9x multiple on FY2026E earnings and a business earning about 14% on equity. Three sourced drivers. First, the margin: the nine months of 2026 earned a 30.2% gross margin on sales of IDR862.9bn against 22.7% a year earlier, a step-up visible in the quarterly filing itself [S6]. Second, the demand pull: the E5 mandate began in July 2026 and E10 is targeted for 2027 against installed ethanol capacity of 78,825kl already running at 92.6% [S3, F5, F3, S8, S9]. Third, the balance sheet: equity of IDR903.4bn at 30 September 2026 on which IDR165.3bn is a PSAK 16 revaluation surplus, so pre-revaluation book is about IDR738.1bn or IDR123 a share against a price of IDR100, roughly 0.81x pre-revaluation book for a business earning a mid-teens return on the reported equity [S6, F21, F37]. We do not argue there is no net debt: there is IDR68.0bn of it at the September reporting date, the seasonal harvest peak, against IDR17.9bn of net cash at the June valuation date [S6, F20, F22]. What the price implies: the reverse DCF cannot bracket the price on growth alone (the lowest sensitivity cell on the growth and margin axes still discounts above the market price), so the market is not discounting growth; it is pricing a permanent return to the FY2024 trough gross margin of 16.6%, which our deepened bear case now models [S4].
